title: Commonwealth v. Cosby
summary: The excerpt holds that fundamental fairness requires enforcement of an unconditional nonprosecution assurance when it induces detrimental surrender of the constitutional privilege against self-incrimination.
notes:
The material involves allegations of sexual assault. The excerpt’s description of the earlier prosecutor’s evaluation is attributed to him and the opinion, not adopted as an independent assessment of the complainant’s credibility.

The omitted disposition: the court vacated Cosby's convictions and sentence and barred any retrial, holding that the Commonwealth could not bait-and-switch after D.A. Castor's February 17, 2005 signed press release induced Cosby to testify in the civil case; the settlement was $3.38 million.

sections.Parties: William Cosby was the criminal defendant appealing convictions arising from Andrea Constand’s allegations. The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania prosecuted him after an earlier district attorney had announced a decision not to prosecute.
sections.Material Facts:
The earlier district attorney concluded that a criminal conviction was unlikely on the evidence then available and sought to facilitate a civil action. According to his later testimony, he communicated a decision not to prosecute so that Cosby could no longer invoke the Fifth Amendment in civil discovery. Cosby’s lawyers understood the decision that way. Cosby then gave four civil depositions without asserting that privilege, and the civil action settled for $3.38 million. The records were later unsealed, and a subsequent prosecution used the changed circumstances.

The announcement and surrounding statements must be read carefully. The reproduced press release includes a statement about reconsidering a decision in the context of public discussion. The assigned excerpt quotes the former prosecutor’s account of an unconditional nonprosecution decision, while also accepting the trial court’s finding that there was no formal immunity contract. Those are distinct evidentiary and legal points.
sections.Procedural History: Cosby sought dismissal based on the earlier assurance. The request was denied; a first trial ended in a mistrial, and the second produced convictions. The supplied portion of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court’s June 30, 2021 opinion addresses enforceability of the assurance on appeal. It stops before the complete application and formal remedial order.
sections.Issue: Can a prosecutor’s unilateral assurance bind later prosecution when no formal immunity bargain exists but the defendant detrimentally relinquishes a constitutional protection in reliance on it?
sections.Holding: The stated rule is that an unconditional nonprosecution promise inducing detrimental surrender of the right not to testify must be enforced as a matter of fundamental fairness and due process. A nonprosecution decision is not automatically enforceable simply because it was made.
sections.Reasoning:
The court accepted the finding that no formal immunity agreement had been proved, then treated the legal consequence of the prosecutor’s actions as a separate question. Contract and promissory-estoppel principles inform the due-process inquiry: foreseeable reliance, actual action in reliance, and resulting injustice matter even without a bargained-for exchange. Prosecutors occupy a public role carrying obligations of fairness toward people whose constitutional choices their assurances influence.

The excerpt distinguishes ordinary charging discretion from an assurance that causes an irreversible change in the defendant’s position. The latter implicates due process even though the prosecutor normally has broad freedom to select or decline charges. The lesson for Contracts is a comparison about promise enforcement and reliance; the criminal constitutional setting prevents mechanically treating the case as an ordinary commercial § 90 damages action.

textbookImport.scope: Assigned edited supplemental excerpt; full application, separate opinions, and formal remedial disposition omitted

learning.why: This assigned remedies reading reaches back to reliance and promise enforcement. It illustrates why a course-wide concept index must cross the syllabus’s unit boundaries.

topics.promissory-estoppel: The court uses foreseeable and detrimental reliance to inform the due-process inquiry.
topics.remedies: Asks why enforcement of an assurance may be necessary after irreversible reliance.
topics.governing-law: Constitutional fairness governs this public-law application of promise principles.
topics.reliance: The enforceability of the non-prosecution assurance rested entirely on Cosby's detrimental reliance in surrendering his Fifth Amendment privilege.
topics.equitable-estoppel: The court's fundamental-fairness rationale is an estoppel against the government, closer to equitable estoppel than to bargain contract.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Wecht wrote for the majority. Justice Dougherty filed a concurring and dissenting opinion, and former Chief Justice Saylor dissented, disagreeing that Castor's press release should produce the majority's result and preferring the narrower remedy of suppressing the evidence derived from the civil depositions rather than barring retrial.

mnemonic.rationale: A press release that became immunity
